How this list is ordered

Four gates, applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — depth of discharge and inverter efficiency — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

The loads this ranks against

A single 1/3–1/2 HP submersible sump pump, on its own. Storms bring other loads with them, but the pump is the one that decides whether the basement floods, and mixing in a fridge or a furnace blower would dilute the one number this page exists to get right: the pump’s own start-up current, which two manufacturers of the same “1/3 HP” pump publish 87% apart from each other. That gap is why this page ranks against the nameplate a reader’s own pump actually carries, not a horsepower rating.

Twelve hours, to match the site’s home-backup default — but this is the one scenario on the site where the target duration cannot change the outcome. No manufacturer publishes how many times a sump pump cycles per hour, because that number depends on how fast groundwater is entering a specific basement, not on the pump — so no station on this page can be shown to last any number of hours on this load, at 4 h or at 48 h alike. What changes with the target is nothing; what this page can prove is whether the pump starts at all.

Why 7 records carry no printable runtime

7 of the 12 records here start and hold this load set and still carry no runtime this page will print, for one reason: BLUETTI, EcoFlow and Jackery publish no depth of discharge and no inverter efficiency for them, so the hours a reader actually wants cannot be computed from anything but the number on the box — and dividing a nameplate by a load is the one thing this site will not do. No brand on this page publishes both figures, so no runtime on this page is a computed one.

What their rows do carry is the bound: that record’s nameplate over this set’s average draw, which is arithmetic anyone can redo against the summary above — floored, never rounded up, so the printed ceiling never claims an hour more than the number supports — and it is printed on those of their rows whose nameplate is published. But it is a ceiling and not a duration: it assumes the pack surrenders every watt-hour printed on it and that the inverter loses nothing turning DC into AC, and no battery does either. The real hours sit somewhere below that ceiling, and the two missing figures are exactly what would say how far below. That is the difference between a number this page will print and a number it will not.

The scope of that finding, stated: as of 2026-08-01 we read each manufacturer’s own published documents for these 7 models and found no depth-of-discharge and no inverter-efficiency figure in them. It is a statement about what those documents contained on that date — not a claim that the number exists nowhere. Send us one that is published and the record moves, and the row moves with it. This is a statement about published data, not about the hardware — the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.

The load that changes the answer

Add a well pump to the same set and the first gate, which was already turning records away, tightens further: not one of the 12 clears it outright — 1 is a tight fit and 11 cannot do it at all. The reason is one instant: a well pump asks for 6,762 W at start-up on its own — 5.9× its own running draw, against 2,650 W for everything on the list above put together. That start-up figure is a published locked-rotor rating for an induction motor of this size. A sump pump’s own measured locked-rotor current is unusually low for a motor its size — well under the NEC table a lot of sizing advice still quotes. A well pump is not the same machine wearing a different label, and this is why you check the nameplate rather than the horsepower. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

How many of the 12 actually run it?
7 of 12 do, and the other 5 are the finding on this page. 920 W of running draw and 2,650 W at the worst start-up instant is what every published US record is measured against, and 5 of 12 run out of ceiling somewhere in it. Which means the buying question splits in two: whether a given machine starts it at all, and only then how long it holds. The rows below answer them in that order. Why is the biggest machine not first?
Because this page ranks by what can be proven about the question it asks. Capacity only counts once a brand publishes what it takes to turn that capacity into hours — depth of discharge and inverter efficiency. 12 of the 12 records here publish neither — the same count the panel above prints as unprovable, and each of those rows says which two figures are missing. Nothing about their electrical performance is being marked down: the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.
What is actually being tested here?
920 W of running draw and 2,650 W at the worst start-up instant, put through the compatibility engine against each machine's continuous output, surge ceiling and inverter waveform. A load above 82% of continuous output drops out of the green whatever else is true. The itemised set, with each figure's source and date, is at the top of this page.
How current are the prices?
Every price on this page carries the date it was last checked, next to the figure. Past fourteen days the page says how old it is rather than showing it as current. Prices move; the ranking above them is recomputed on every build from the same records.

No. Nothing on this page can be bought into: the order is the four-gate rule printed above the list, applied to every published record in this region. The one buy link on this page goes to the record the rule selected.
